detail:
The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) describes COPD research as work it leads and supports in the United States and around the world. Research supported by the NHLBI has shown that certain treatments and lifestyle changes, such as quitting smoking, can help people with COPD stay more active and slow the progression of the disease, and current studies look at the potential benefits of treating COPD in its earliest stages. The CAPTURE study validated a simple tool for COPD screening in primary care settings, pairing a quick breathing test with a simple questionnaire, to identify people with undiagnosed COPD so they can receive a diagnosis and start to get treatment.

Other NHLBI-funded research examines how COPD develops. SPIROMICS II uses information from lung tests, biological specimens, imaging, and genetic testing to help understand what raises a person's risk of COPD and how COPD develops, and to identify biomarkers to predict COPD symptoms and progression. SOURCE, the SPIROMICS Study of Early COPD Progression, looks for the earliest signs of COPD, using questionnaires, breathing tests, imaging, and biospecimens to study how people with a history of smoking develop lung obstruction and why some people develop COPD and others do not. The Pulmonary Trials Cooperative brings together patients, researchers, and healthcare professionals from more than 50 institutions with the common goal of developing new treatments for lung diseases, and the program includes three clinical trials on COPD.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about COPD research and population data.

title: COPD: how NHLBI research is studying the disease in its earliest stages
